planting.note: Drill into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late fall for dormant-season establishment; this long-lived bunchgrass needs no annual termination and is typically grazed or mowed rather than incorporated.

directions: A hybrid between two crested wheatgrass types selected for faster seedling emergence and stronger stand establishment than older strains, 'Hycrest' is drilled at a light rate into disturbed or degraded rangeland soil where it quickly knits together a fibrous root mat that slows wind and water erosion on dry western sites. It greens up earlier in spring than most native bunchgrasses, giving livestock or wildlife an early grazing window while out-competing invasive annual grasses for moisture. Because it is a persistent perennial, no yearly reseeding or tillage termination is needed once a stand is established; management is simply rotational grazing or periodic mowing to keep it vigorous.

planting.note: Seed shallowly into a firm bed on saline or alkaline ground in fall or very early spring; stands persist for many years and are managed by periodic haying or grazing rather than replanted.

directions: Released decades ago for reclaiming saline seep and alkaline ground where few other forages survive, 'Alkar' tall wheatgrass forms coarse, deep-rooted clumps that draw down shallow saline water tables and gradually make the surface soil more workable over several seasons. It is commonly seeded in strips or borders around cropland affected by seep salinity, doubling as a windbreak and a roughage forage once established. Because it is a long-lived perennial, it is not tilled under like an annual cover crop; instead it is cut for hay or grazed, and replanting is only needed if a stand is deliberately removed.

planting.note: Scarify seed and inoculate with the appropriate rhizobium before drilling into lean, disturbed soil; the planting is slow to close the first year or two but then persists for decades without reseeding.

directions: Selected by a USDA plant materials program specifically for mine-spoil and roadcut reclamation, 'Lathco' flatpea is a nitrogen-fixing perennial legume that sprawls into a dense, tangled groundcover rather than climbing, binding thin or infertile subsoil against erosion where turf grasses struggle to take hold. It establishes slowly, often needing a full season or two before it knits together a weed-suppressing mat, so it is usually seeded with a nurse grass for quicker initial cover. Once mature it requires essentially no maintenance or termination, persisting as a permanent low-fertility soil stabilizer that steadily adds organic matter and fixed nitrogen to degraded ground.
sources: USDA Soil Conservation Service Plant Materials Center
